abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a foundational reformulation of the model checking problem for infinite-state systems using game-theoretic semantics and alternating automata theory. Traditional approaches to temporal logic verification rely on fixpoint computations over finite state spaces, which fundamentally break down when confronted with parameterized systems, pushdown processes, or lossy channel protocols. We propose a novel framework based on distributive justice automata that provides a unified perspective on fairness, recursion, and state-space abstraction. Our central contribution establishes that the satisfaction relation for CTL* specifications over well-structured transition systems admits a characterization as the winning condition of a parity game with polynomially bounded arena size. This theoretical breakthrough enables a new class of symbolic algorithms that avoid explicit state enumeration. We further demonstrate that the decision problem for the mu-calculus with nested least and greatest fixpoints reduces to solving games of bounded treewidth. These results open a paradigm shift in automated reasoning by replacing enumeration-based model checking with structure-preserving transformations. Complexity analysis reveals that our approach achieves PSPACE completeness for a broad class of infinite-state specifications, significantly improving upon prior exponential upper bounds.

We establish tighter complexity bounds for quantified Boolean formulas with restricted quantifier prefixes arising in verification applications. While the general QBF decision problem remains PSPACE-complete, practical instances from bounded model checking and program synthesis exhibit structural patterns that have not been fully exploited theoretically. Our analysis focuses on hypergraph-prefix QBF where quantifiers are organized according to variable dependencies, a fragment that captures many real-world encodings. We prove that this fragment is NEXP-complete and provide a constructive algorithm achieving optimal performance through hypergraph decomposition. The key insight involves a refined treewidth analysis of the primal variable graph combined with a novel quantification strategy that exploits locality of constraints. For the special case of linear QBF with path-shaped quantifier prefixes, we achieve polynomial-time decidability, improving upon the previous best cubic bound. Our lower bound construction demonstrates that these improvements are optimal under standard complexity assumptions. Experimental validation on benchmark formulas confirms that our theoretical complexity improvements translate directly to empirical speedups when integrated with state-of-the-art QBF solvers.

We present λVerify, a new interactive theorem proving architecture fundamentally grounded in contextual modal type theory rather than the traditional Martin-Löf tradition. The core innovation lies in our novel modal machinery that natively supports both temporal and spatial reasoning within the same logical framework, enabling direct formalization of distributed protocols and concurrent data structures. Unlike existing systems such as Coq or Agda, λVerify implements a two-level kernel architecture where the inner level handles definitional equality through a persistent union-find data structure, while the outer level manages modal contexts with incremental dependency tracking. Our proof search engine combines bottom-up unification with top-down goal decomposition, guided by a learned heuristic scoring function trained on large proof corpora. The system features a domain-specific tactic language that compiles to primitive inference rules with verified compilation correctness. We demonstrate λVerify's effectiveness through complete formalizations of the Raft consensus algorithm, cache coherence protocols, and a formally verified hypervisor. Benchmarks show a 40% reduction in proof script length compared to equivalent Coq developments while maintaining comparable automation levels.

We describe substantial engineering advances in Description Logic reasoning through a comprehensive reimplementation of the ELK reasoner with a focus on large-scale ontology classification. Our system introduces a novel lazy unfolding strategy that defers concept absorption until classification time, combined with an optimized rule compilation phase that eliminates redundant axioms through term rewriting. The critical improvement lies in our incremental saturation algorithm, which maintains partial classification results across ontology updates by exploiting the lattice-theoretic structure of the subsumption hierarchy. We employ a concurrent architecture with work-stealing schedulers for parallel rule application, achieving near-linear speedup on multi-core hardware. Memory consumption is reduced through aggressive garbage collection of intermediate results and compression of derived rules using minimal perfect hashing. Experimental evaluation on the complete OWL 2 EL profile benchmarks demonstrates a mean speedup of 8.3x over the previous ELK implementation and competitive performance against specialized reasoners for larger ontologies. The system handles ontologies with millions of axioms that previously caused out-of-memory failures, making expressive DL reasoning practical for industrial-scale knowledge management applications.
